epTitle: Preparing Young Scholars for Higher Ed
transcript: [MUSIC] Hello and welcome to this episode of This Epic Life, the podcast. I'm Bailey Bennett Andrade here along with CEO of Epic Education, Dr. Nancy Dome. Today we are talking with Nicholas Hastings, who is the Executive Director at Square root Academy. Thank you for being here today with us Nicholas. >> Thank you. Pleasure to be here. So thank you all for having me. >> Absolutely. So we want to start off, could you just give us a little rundown of what you're doing over there at Square root Academy? >> Sure, so I'll tell a little bit of background on what we do here at Square root Academy and a little bit about our beginnings. So Square root Academy was a concept imagined by me and my co-founders when we were undergrads. A couple of us went to Sac State, another one is also an Intel engineer. So we kind of put our hats together and really came up with an idea of making sure that we were serving underrepresented populations and exposing them to STEM based education and experiences. During our undergrad years and our time in industry, there was very little representation, very few places where we actually seen people that reflected us visually and culturally. So we began to kind of like ponder why that is. And it's not because there is any innate lack of genius, but more so lack of opportunity in our neighborhoods to really get access to this quality of education. So we sat on this concept for a while, we thought on it. And in 2016, we started Square root Academy to address this issue kind of head on. We started off initially serving a school in my neighborhood that I grew up in South Sacramento, a small community called Mediview. Going there, serving kids, complete free education to make sure that the access was there, offered it at no cost to make sure the kids were able to actually participate. Basically trying to remove all those barriers to educate those kids. So that first year, we hit about 52 scholars, which was, we were we're ecstatic. We're super excited that we were able to serve 52 kids. Fast forward nearly four years later, we serve a little over 4,000 kids. And that's across various school districts within Sacramento and the surrounding regions. Also including kind of like our special events such as Great STEM Summit, Active Park, 5,000 Watts, really making sure that we are exposing kids to STEM. Not just in a way that is digestible for one type of kid, but in a way that works for the kids that are more theory based, the ones that are more practical applications. The one that want to use STEM for maybe developing art projects. Our goal really is to expose them to the different avenues that they can take and empower them to have the choice to pursue whatever option they choose. And so you really are tapping into learning modalities and so however they learn and then having that kind of merge with learning the STEM piece of it as well. So how do you deliver the content? Is it after school programs? Is it do you come in during school time? How does that work? Well, Nancy, let me tell you. >> [LAUGH] We offer our programming in a wide array of manners here. So we have STEM and Richmond series. I add three different levels. Our main bread and butter is our signature events and our STEM and Richmond series. So STEM and Richmond series comes in at three levels, serving fifth through 12th grade scholars. So we have STEM and Richmond series one where we expose them to 3D modeling, a little bit of coding, physics, chemistry, just a wide breadth of STEM. So they can just get it all in one quick go. We implement that in schools during the school day, sometimes after school, sometimes zero period in community centers out of our own co-working space, lab seven co-working in various different places. So that's SES one. SES two is a little more specified where we may be teaching the kids about a single subject for an entire school year or academic semester. We've done things like teaching kids about cybersecurity. We also, one that I really enjoyed, was our renewable energy systems one, where we taught our kids how to make solar energy pretty much in a suitcase, and then we shifted off to developing nations. So now they're becoming a whole humanitarians and we're teaching them the human element of technology beyond what they typically teach, which is more the cut and dry. So we're teaching them to recognize the impact of what they're creating, beyond just the technical sense, if that makes sense here. But then once they get to this collegiate environment, it's a completely different one from what they actually grew up in. So sometimes, I can speak for myself included, you start to develop a little bit of imposter syndrome and ask me yourself, do I actually belong here? So what we do is we make sure to equip them with the confidence necessary to know that they do belong here. Not only do they belong here, they have a voice here and it is important. So we make sure to teach them all of that during that. And also in partnership with Los Rios School District, our kids are also receiving college credit for going through. >> Nice. >> So they know that they can do it because they've already done it. It's just a different environment. So that would be how we actually implement our programming. Our other signature events are pretty much just imagined by us and dished out on a quarterly basis, which I love doing. >> [LAUGH] >> Super fun stuff. >> Yeah, well, it just is amazing. And I really appreciate that you have this follow on, right? This mentor piece that really supports them because I think that, that is where we will typically fall short is that in schools that have really made a commitment to exposing our youth to different fields of study. They still miss that marker, which is when they leave, what happens when they leave your space, right? And they go into the space where all of a sudden they don't see themselves anymore. And then there's all this messaging, whether it's explicit or implicit, that's giving them the message that they don't belong there, they're not good enough. And so how do we support them to stay? So I think that mentoring component, I wish more people would implement it because I think it would be seriously a life changing factor for some of our kids to have that kind of support. >> Well, it's needed, we have to instill it in them early because in a lot of cases, these kids are first generation. So they can't necessarily get the level of support they needed in the home, not because the people in the home don't necessarily want to, because they simply do not know what our kids are up against when they're transitioning into this next level of academia. So it takes mentors and people that have kind of been there before to be able to say, hey, this is how you get it done. >> Yeah. >> I can make it. >> Yeah. >> We want to make sure to be that connecting bridge for those kids in a time that's super pivotal in their life where they will need this the most. >> Yeah. >> Yeah. >> Right. So Nicholas, when you started off your career, you started off as an engineer, right? And then you noticed that there was this equity piece that needed to be woven into it. And then worked in full store as I owned a car dealership. I did freelance engineering. I actually taught a lot of this stuff previously before I even kind of realized that this is what I wanted to do. So when I was a kid and when I was younger growing up, you know, I always knew I had two goals in mind. Become an engineer and then possibly give back to my community. Those things kind of just carried me and I think that those were really how this whole Screwood Academy thing kind of came to be of course with the assistants and with the strong support of our collaborators here. It was really the ideology that this is the current situation, but it can be better. And that mentality kind of like carried me and got me through college. And then it made us really realize, you know, the importance of doing what we're doing at Screwood Academy and other organizations like it. You know, we, there's always a lot of times where it's like, hey, somebody should do something about that. You are that person and we were those people. So it's we recognize that there was an issue and a deficit in our communities that we were perfectly equipped to solve. So Screwood Academy, I started out with Screwood Academy while I was still actually an industry. So I was still an industry working as an engineer when this whole thing came out to be. You have representation of somebody that looks like you from the same place issue that has done it. You can do the same thing. Yeah. I don't think I would feel as confident telling them that message not having gone through it. So zero regrets. I think that it happened just the way that it was supposed to for us to be able to have the impact on our community that we would like to have. Mm hmm. Yeah. What was your support? Like, what was your inspiration to get you through that? Because engineering as a Black young man is not something that you would see highly represented even today. So yeah, it sucked. Yeah. I'm like, let's just be honest about it. When people are like, oh, yeah, college is some of the best years of my life, that is not going to be the case for engineering. And that's okay. Yeah. You know, when it's it's, you know, you'll build these strong relationships, these strong connections, you'll have a good time. But, you know, I don't go into this telling my telling my kids that this is anything less than hard work. Yeah. No, it does take hard work, you know, for the reward that's at the end of all of this, you have to be willing to put in the work. You can't have a dream and not act on it and expect it to come through and come to fruition. You actually have to put in the hour. So college was definitely, definitely one of the tougher times for me. It was a tough time being first generation. Um, didn't have a whole heck of a lot of family support, but within the university, I did find my community. I found kind of a different family for myself on that campus. One of them is actually my co-founders. Um, you know, I found this organization called National Society of Black Engineers. And, um, I became deeply involved with that, you know, vice president, president, served on the regional executive board and really just kind of kept in close quarters with them, as well as the other organizations, um, focused on marginalized populations such as the Society of Hispanic Professional Engineers, Society of Women Engineers, all worked very closely together. We studied together. We shared resources, um, because it was just a more relatable community. Yeah. And when you go into these classes, you're not going to see a lot of people that understand you culturally. Mm-hmm. So you kind of have to like seek out and really take an active role in pursuing your own community, you know? Mm-hmm. How did you figure out how to be an educator once you decided to switch from industry to education? I have a number of thoughts on that. Mm-hmm. I think there are some things that are being implemented in school already that are no brainers that we should probably get rid of, um, especially considering that a lot of our current educational system, Common Core and all of that, is in response to the Industrial Revolution that came out. And we were adjusted. The world is different. We were training people to be workers, not thinkers, not inquisitive, not to leverage their imagination. Mm-hmm. And we never changed that. Mm-hmm. I don't know who that makes sense to, but it did not make sense to me. Mm-hmm. So, for one, just kind of adopted some of the things that I've seen wrong with the school system and said, "Hey, we want to build something differently around this." So, I leveraged a few different people. For one, we actually have active engineers queue-seeing our curriculum just to make sure that things are actually up to a relevancy of what's actually going to be used in industry. We have teachers and professors at the University of Sac State in the engineering department, also vetting our curriculum. We also read several books and several studies on how to really make this effective while leveraging our own educational experience to tailor one for our kids and our population here. Now, do we have the best pedagogy? I'm not entirely sure. But it is a pedagogy that I know to be effective within our populations. So everything that we do is hands-on application. And that was directly informed from speaking to the PGEs, the Intel's of saying that while the theoretical is great, it's great to know for research and things like that, that they really want people that know how to apply these theories towards a tangible solution. We did a program, goodness, we've done this a few times, where we take a group of kids, we teach them the technical skills to be successful, and then we say, "Okay, kid." Now we want you in your small group to apply this toward the tangible community solution here, so letting them actually develop community solutions and power them and showing them you can make a difference in your community through tech. We've got some great projects. I think the most recent one was a kid, a group of kids, they built out a website to kind of help out connect other young people with mental wellness offerings. We also had another group. They made a prototype of it. They called it the boat dozer. So it's kind of helping in the environment. So Ruby instilling a strong human element in STEM, where it's normally kind of cold and calculated. Well, you said something earlier, you called it Global Humanitarians, and I job at that down, and that phrase resonates with me about how we are teaching our kids to be contributors to society, and that that should be a part of our work. What's interesting though, is that, and this is a little bit of a tangent, but, and I shouldn't say but, I should say and, this notion that within communities of color though, we always are striving to look at how to be better humanitarians, and this is, I think this is a lesson that needs to go across the board and be part of the lessons that we do in our Y communities about this notion that we're all connected and that your success supports my success, and that there is no lack, right? But yeah, I think mostly just also kind of understanding the differences between the kids that they're having actually come on board here. I would say that's one thing that I can just think about the top of my head. Yeah, I appreciate that. Thank you. I've got some years on you, and it hasn't. epTitle: Distance Learning Exposing the Digital Divide
transcript: [MUSIC] >> Hello everyone. I'm Bailey Bennett Andrade here with CEO of Epic Education, Dr. Nancy Dome. Today we are talking with principal at San Diego County Office of Education, Dr. Leila Kerpindall. How are you doing, Leila? >> I'm doing well. How are you? >> We're doing pretty good, I would say. Hey, hang it in there. >> Yeah, that's all we can do at this point. >> Exactly. >> So today we wanted to get some of your input on what's going on in our world of distance learning that we have very quickly had to transition to since the COVID-19 breakout and pandemic.
